title: GreenWave Health - migration planning: OpenAI -> Redwood evaluation
summary: Discovery call focused on migrating GreenWave's production chat and summarization pipelines from OpenAI-managed endpoints to Redwood Hosted and then Dedicated/Private. Discussed compatibility risks (tokenization, sampling parity), benchmarking (p50/p95 latency, throughput), private deployment options (VPC, KMS), and next steps for a pilot including eval parity runs and benchmark spreadsheet.
next_steps: Redwood to share migration checklist + model mapping spreadsheet (Alex) by 2025-11-24
Customer to provide three representative prompts and a small evaluation corpus (Marcus) by 2025-11-26
Schedule benchmarking slot on Redwood Hosted for parity test (Priya) week of 2025-11-25
Security follow-up: share SOC2 summary + KMS integration doc (Jordan) by 2025-11-24
action_items: Alex Kim | Send model mapping + quickstart for stream vs non-stream endpoints | 2025-11-24
Priya Shen | Run initial throughput test (200 concurrent streams) on Hosted and capture p50/p95 | 2025-11-26
Marcus Lee | Provide eval corpus (1000 examples) + top-10 prompt set | 2025-11-26

Sana Rao | Share required compliance documents list (data residency, retention) | 2025-11-24
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-11-21 14:00 PST | Duration: 44 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood EngOps), Marcus (Head of ML - GreenWave), Dana (CTO), Jamie (Platform), Sana (Security), Tom (Product)

00:00 Alex Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, from Redwood — I'm Alex, I'm the AE on this account. Priya from solutions is here, Jordan from EngOps. How's everyone doing?
00:12 Marcus Lee: Good, thanks. Busy day, appreciate you making time.
00:15 Alex Kim: Cool. Quick agenda: we wanted to understand your current setup with OpenAI, what pain points you're seeing, and map out a migration plan — hosted first, then evaluate Dedicated or Private. Is that right?
00:26 Dana Ortiz: Yeah that's it. We run two main pipelines: a customer-facing chat product and an internal clinical summarization pipeline. Both currently call OpenAI's API. Latency and cost are getting concerning as usage grows.
00:39 Priya Shen: Got it — can you give a sense of current RPS and token distribution? Even ballparks help.
00:45 Jamie Park: For chat peak we see about 80 reqs/s, average 600 tokens per response, spikes to ~2000 tokens for long summaries. For summarization job runs batch at night — throughput matters there, but latency isn't as strict.
01:03 Tom Bennett: And cost — OpenAI is fine early on but it scales roughly linear and we want options to tune quantization and batching.
01:11 Alex Kim: Makes sense. Two quick clarifiers: are you using function calling / structured outputs today? And are you tied to a particular model family at OpenAI?
01:19 Marcus Lee: Yes, we use function calls heavily for the chat layer. We're on gpt-4o for certain flows, gpt-3.5 for others. We also experimented with Anthropic for safety but it's not prod.
01:29 Priya Shen: Important to surface: function calling and response schema changes can cause behavior drift when you switch runtimes — we typically do an eval parity run where we re-run your prompt set across models and compare key metrics.
01:39 Marcus Lee: We want that. Our big fear is non-determinism — even small tokenization differences or sampling seeds can change downstream QA flags.
01:47 Jordan Li: Also curious about KV cache / prefix caching — our chat sessions have long context windows and we rely on KV cache behaviour to hit latency targets. How comparable is Redwood's runtime to vLLM/TGI-style caches?
02:00 Priya Shen: Good question. Redwood's runtime has a KV cache optimized for GPU inference; in Hosted we support persistent prefix cache and session-affine routing so long sessions can be kept warm. Implementation details differ from vLLM but we provide comparable hit-rate guarantees and observability — we'll show cache metrics in the console.
02:18 Jamie Park: And for Dedicated/Private — do you ship the same caching? Are there differences on prem?
02:24 Priya Shen: The runtime is the same codepath. On Private deployments we run with customer networking constraints; the KV cache can be local to the serving pool and we support optional encryption at rest for cached keys.
02:35 Sana Rao: On encryption — KMS integration is a requirement. Our policy requires that model keys and any PII are encrypted with our KMS, and we need audit logs for every request.
02:45 Jordan Li: Also SSO for the console, RBAC for routes.
02:49 Alex Kim: We support SAML SSO and RBAC. For KMS, Private and Dedicated can integrate with your AWS KMS or other providers via bring-your-own-key. For Hosted, we offer customer-managed keys in select regions — we can map this to your compliance needs. We'll share the SOC2 summary and KMS onboarding doc after this call.
03:05 Dana Ortiz: Great. Can you talk about model compatibility? We use a few custom prompt templates that rely on token offsets and ability to do deterministic sampling when needed.
03:15 Priya Shen: Two things: tokenizer differences (OpenAI uses cl100k_base; many open models use different BPE). We usually run a tokenizer layer compatibility check and can provide a token-mapping table. For sampling, Redwood's runtime exposes the same temperature/top-p params. Absolute determinism is hard across different model families — if you need byte-for-byte parity we recommend deploying the same model weights (or a certified equivalent) and pinning seeds, but small divergence is expected if you change model families.
03:43 Marcus Lee: We're evaluating options: keep hosted but switch to Redwood hosted endpoints to avoid re-architecting; or move to Dedicated for predictable latency and cost; or Private for data residency. What's the tradeoff?
03:53 Alex Kim: Hosted is lowest friction — quick onboarding, you run your parity evals on our hosted infra. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity, lower tail latencies under commit, and predictable unit economics. Private adds VPC/on-prem for data residency and full KMS control but has a longer setup time. Many customers start Hosted for parity tests then commit to Dedicated once they've validated throughput and cost.
04:15 Marcus Lee: We also run nightly batch summarization using TGI clusters today — we care about throughput there. Can Redwood match TGI for throughput at lower cost?
04:25 Priya Shen: We have benchmarking numbers but it depends on quantization (INT8 vs FP16), batch sizes, sequence lengths. For long sequences, our kernel selection optimizes attention patterns; and with continuous batching for batch jobs we often outperform vanilla TGI setups because of optimizations at the runtime layer. We'll run a bench using your average seq len sample to prove it.
04:45 Tom Bennett: On evaluation — how do you do score parity? We use ROUGE/BLEU, but for conversation we have human evals and compliance filters.
04:52 Priya Shen: We compare multiple axes: token-level parity, sampling divergence, response correctness, latency metrics. For safety/compliance, we can re-run your classifier and safety filters against Redwood outputs. We usually provide a spreadsheet with side-by-side comparisons and a delta analysis.
05:07 Marcus Lee: Perfect. Another technical worry: streaming behavior. Our UI expects incremental tokens over a websocket. OpenAI streams token deltas we rely on. Does Redwood match that?
05:17 Alex Kim: Yes — Redwood supports streaming with chunked token frames over both REST and websocket SDKs. There can be slight framing differences but we provide a stream compatibility shim and examples in the quickstart. We'll send a short demo snippet.
05:31 Jamie Park: Any differences in rate limits or soft throttling? We had issues when we hit bursts.
05:36 Alex Kim: In Hosted we have per-key quotas and soft-burst policies; for Dedicated we can configure higher per-tenant concurrency and autoscaling within the reserved pool. We'll work with you to size the Dedicated commit based on peak QPS and token throughput.
05:50 Sana Rao: On privacy — does Redwood store request logs? How long, and can that be disabled for Private?
05:57 Jordan Li: For Hosted we have retention settings; data retention can be adjusted and we support no-storage options for sensitive routes. Private deployments give you full control. We'll include retention options in the checklist.
06:08 Marcus Lee: Cool. Let's talk about the pilot: timeline and what success looks like.
06:13 Priya Shen: Pilot flow we recommend: 1) provide prompt set and eval corpus, 2) Redwood runs parity and throughput benchmarks on Hosted, 3) compare deltas, iterate on prompt engineering, 4) if parity acceptable, spin up Dedicated sizing test or Private PoC. Typical pilot is 2–4 weeks.
06:25 Marcus Lee: Our goal: p95 latency <= 450ms for chat short flows; for summarization p50 throughput >= 5k tokens/sec for batch windows. Also cost needs to be <= 60% of our current OpenAI spend for high-volume flows to justify migration.
06:40 Priya Shen: Noted. We'll capture those SLOs in the bench plan. For the cost target, we'll show cost per token with and without quantization and caching.
06:48 Tom Bennett: What about model updates and rollouts? We need canaries and automatic fallback in case of regressions.
06:55 Alex Kim: Redwood Console supports rollouts: canary percentages, A/B, and automatic fallback to a stable variant if quality drops. We can also tie regressions to prompt sets and alert you.
07:06 Jamie Park: Do you support model pinning and versioned artifacts?
07:09 Priya Shen: Yes, model pinning and immutable model versions for rollouts. You can pin a route to an exact model hash and then promote new versions gradually.
07:17 Marcus Lee: Network question: we need VPC peering and egress constraints — can Redwood Dedicated be deployed inside our account or do we have to do a VPN?
07:25 Jordan Li: There are two options: Dedicated in our cloud account with a peering/VPN, or Private where the control plane is customer-managed. For Dedicated we can do customer VPC peering for data plane traffic in supported cloud regions. We'll collect your CIDR ranges and constraints.
07:36 Sana Rao: Also need pen-test certifications and a timeline to complete a security review.
07:40 Alex Kim: We'll include our latest pen-test summary and SOC2 report in the security packet. For deeper audits we'll schedule our security reps.
07:48 Marcus Lee: Great. A few implementation details: tokenization mismatch — can you show an automated tokenizer diff tool?
07:54 Priya Shen: Yes, we run a tokenizer diff that highlights token counts differences per prompt and map UI-level offsets back to tokens. It's part of our migration checklist.
08:03 Tom Bennett: And for streaming, any guidance for re-assembly of chunks if you change streaming framing? We have client-side logic fragile to framing changes.
08:11 Alex Kim: We'll provide a client-side compatibility shim and sample SDK changes required for minimal updates. We'll also test your UI flows during the pilot.
08:20 Marcus Lee: Ok, next — pricing model for Dedicated sizing: do you charge per reserved GPU hour or per-token on top?
08:27 Alex Kim: Dedicated is primarily reserved capacity with a monthly commit; usage above commit is billed at a discounted overage rate. We can model your cost in the pricing spreadsheet using your traffic numbers.
08:36 Jamie Park: Any gotchas migrating from TGI-managed infra for batch? We use some custom batching logic.
08:41 Priya Shen: The runtime can accept batching hints and we have config for max batch size/timeout. We'll need to validate your batching logic in bench runs — sometimes tuning the timeout window yields significant cost savings.
08:53 Marcus Lee: Alright. Can we commit to the following: we'll send the eval corpus and prompt list by Wednesday; Redwood will run parity and a throughput bench on Hosted by next Monday; security docs by Tuesday?
09:03 Alex Kim: Yes — Alex will send the checklist and skeleton bench spreadsheet by Monday 2025-11-24, Priya will schedule the bench slot once the corpus is uploaded. Jordan will share KMS and network onboarding docs.
09:13 Dana Ortiz: Sounds good. Any initial concerns from your side?
09:16 Priya Shen: Only that we get representative traffic — synthetic tests can mislead. Real request shapes (seq len distribution, concurrency patterns) matter. Also if you rely on exact token offsets in downstream tooling we need to map those carefully.
09:28 Marcus Lee: We'll try to provide both production logs sanitized and a smaller live traffic dump.
09:33 Alex Kim: Perfect. I'll follow up with a calendar invite for the bench slot and attach the security packet.
09:38 Tom Bennett: Thanks, everyone.
09:40 Alex Kim: Thanks all, we'll send the next items. Talk soon.

Meeting end.
